About: spontaneous symmetry breaking in the 2D Ising ferromagnet

Source

Concept
2D square-lattice Ising model, exact Metropolis dynamics (J = kB = 1, periodic L×L lattice). Whether — and at what temperature — order appears is exactly what the inquiry has you measure for yourself.
Serves
Statistical mechanics / phase transitions: order parameter, critical temperature, critical fluctuations and slowing down, finite-size effects.
Inquiry
Predict the outcome of slow cooling, then the behaviour of the signed trace near Tc; measure ⟨|M|⟩ yourself and place your own Tc guess before the exact curve is shown.
Misconception
"Order needs an organiser — something must favour up." Does it? The inquiry's prediction cards put exactly that to the test — cool the grid and watch. (The outcome fills in here once the inquiry is complete.)

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealTwo gated prediction cards; each distractor is a real student intuition (order needs a field, symmetry forces a 50/50 split, "up" is preferred).
Invariant made visibleThe rule's up/down symmetry never changes; only the run's outcome does — the signed trace records the choice run after run.
Operational numbersEvery displayed number is measured from the live lattice or computed from the exact kernel formulas, with units in J/kB.
Honest dataThe finite-grid tail above Tc is shown, never subtracted; the exact infinite-lattice curve is labelled and sits below the hot-side dots.
Felt physicsThe record ring counts sweeps, and near the transition a measurement deliberately takes ×3 the sweeps — successive sweeps decorrelate slowly there, so the honest price of a clean average is felt as a longer wait.
Formal layer optionalMetropolis rule, Onsager Tc, M(T) and the finite-size shift live behind ⚛︎ The Physics, the pop-up revision sheet.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A hot grid of stubborn neighbours

Let’s meet the grid. Each spin gains only by matching its four neighbours — nothing in the rule prefers up or down. The grid starts hot at T = 3.0 J/kB. Press ▶ Play and watch the mess shimmer.

2 · Predict: what does slow cooling make?

Now for your first prediction. Suppose you cool slowly to T = 1.6 J/kB and wait. What do you think the settled grid will look like?

3 · Cool it and watch

Let’s cool it. Drag T slowly down toward 1.6 J/kB and watch patches of both colours grow, merge and fight. Keep an eye on the signed M trace as one colour takes the frame.

4 · Symmetry in the rule, choice in the run

Isn’t that remarkable? Order appeared with no organiser. Now drag T back up to 3.0 — let the grid scramble to fresh noise — then cool once more. The trace’s sign records which way this run chose.

5 · Predict: the trace at T = 2.30

Here’s a subtler one. Suppose you park T at 2.30 J/kB and leave it there. What do you think the signed M trace will do?

6 · Where deciding is slow

Let’s see. Set T ≈ 2.30 and watch the trace wander. Then press ⏺ Record: successive sweeps decorrelate so slowly here that the measurement takes ×3 the sweeps — the ring shows you that price.

7 · Measure, map, then reveal

Now you get to be the experimenter. Record ⟨|M|⟩ at six or more temperatures, spanning clearly-ordered and clearly-mixed. Drag the flag to where the rise begins — the exact curve appears only once your map is in. Then rerun at L = 32: does the rise move? Which way? And before the reveal, where do you think the exact transition sits?

8 · Why a toy carries real physics

Let’s zoom out. Magnets, liquid–vapour, alloys: all order this way near their critical points. Systems that share a dimension and a symmetry even share the same exponents, so a real 3D fluid follows the 3D Ising values, not this 2D grid’s. A liquid near its critical point shows the same slow, large swings — so what do you think plays the role of M there?

Why |M|?

▾

Trace shows signed M; the plot uses |M| — up and down order count the same.

Metropolis rule, J = kB = 1. ΔE ≤ 0 is accepted with probability exactly 1; one sweep = L² attempted flips.
Onsager's exact critical point — the self-dual condition sinh(2J/kBTc) = 1.
Exact spontaneous magnetisation (Onsager–Yang). The exponent is β = 1/8 exactly, not mean-field's 1/2, and not a fit.
Finite-size shift with ν = 1 (exact in 2D) and empirical amplitude a ≈ 0.8: a finite grid finds the transition warm, by ≈ Tc·0.8/L.

The Physics

Ising order · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A square grid of spins, each up or down, is the simplest model of a magnet. This sim lets you set the temperature, watch the grid rearrange under one local rule, and measure how aligned the whole grid is.

What you'll learn

  • How one spin flip is decided from its energy cost and the temperature.
  • How the average magnetisation ⟨|M|⟩ depends on T, and where it starts to rise.
  • What the signed trace M and the plotted ⟨|M|⟩ each measure.
  • How the grid size L changes what you measure near the transition.
A flip is judged from the spin and its four neighbours alone.

What's on screen

  • Spin up (+1): blue squares in the lattice. The title line above it gives L and T.
  • Spin down (−1): amber squares.
  • M trace (teal): the signed mean spin of the whole grid over the last 15 s, from −1 (all down) to +1 (all up).
  • ⟨|M|⟩ plot (orange dots): one dot per ⏺ Record, with a bar for the sweep-to-sweep spread. Filled dots were measured on the current grid size, hollow ones on another.
  • Exact curve and Tc lines (amber): Onsager's result for an infinite lattice, and where your grid's rise is expected. The Guided Inquiry reveals them after you have mapped the rise yourself.
See itPut the grid at T = 3.0 J/kB. Watch for: both colours mixed in small patches, a few spins across, that keep changing.

Fixed: J = kB = 1, zero external field, periodic edges.

03

A flip is judged by its energy cost

A neighbouring pair contributes −J to the energy if its two spins match and +J if they differ. Each step picks one spin at random and proposes to flip it. The Metropolis rule accepts the flip with this probability:

J = kB = 1. On a square lattice ΔE can only take these five values.
A worked example, and the probabilities at two temperatures.
  • A flip that lowers or keeps the energy is always accepted.
  • An uphill flip is accepted with probability e−ΔE/kBT. For ΔE = +4J that is 0.082 at T = 1.6 and 0.264 at T = 3.0, so heat is what buys disagreement.
  • One sweep is L² attempts: Monte Carlo time, not seconds.
  • This rule satisfies detailed balance, so a long run samples the equilibrium distribution at temperature T.
See itHeat a fresh grid at T = 3.0, then drop to T = 1.6. Watch for: the single-spin flicker thinning out as patches of one colour start to grow.
04

Below Tc the whole grid orders

Below one temperature, matching neighbours win often enough that agreement spreads across the whole grid. Onsager's exact solution for an infinite lattice gives that temperature and the size of the order:

The critical temperature.
The exact magnetisation. The exponent 1/8 is exact in two dimensions.
T L

These sliders move the sim too.

  • M(T) is 0.98 at T = 1.6, and 0.91 at T = 2.0.
  • An eighth root rises steeply: 1% below Tc it is already 0.69, and 0.1% below it is still 0.52.
  • Cool gradually. A sudden quench can freeze the grid into two ordered stripes with domain walls, and the sim flags trapped stripes. Reheat and cool again.
See itCool a 32 × 32 grid in stages from 3.0 to 1.6, then Record. Watch for: the whole lattice settling to one colour, and a recorded ⟨|M|⟩ close to the exact 0.98.
05

Which direction wins is chance

With no external field, flipping every spin leaves the energy and every flip probability unchanged. Nothing in the rule prefers up, so the colour that takes over is decided by each run's random fluctuations, and both are equally likely.

The trace keeps the sign. Each plotted dot is a time average of the size.
  • On a finite grid at zero field, the long-run average of the signed M is exactly zero: given enough time, a grid below Tc flips between its two ordered states.
  • That waiting time grows exponentially with L. Well below Tc it is far longer than any session, so the trace stays at one sign.
  • That is why the plot averages |M|. The signed average would cancel to zero and hide the order, while |M| counts up-order and down-order alike.
See itHeat the 32 × 32 grid back to 3.0 and run the staged cooling again. Watch for: the M trace ending near +1 or near −1, and the recorded ⟨|M|⟩ positive and close to 0.98 either way.
06

Near Tc the grid decides slowly

Close to Tc, ordered patches of every size coexist, and the grid needs very many sweeps before it forgets its present state. The signed M wanders slowly over a wide range instead of jittering about zero.

  • Successive sweeps stay correlated, so 400 sweeps hold far fewer independent samples than they do at T = 1.6 or 3.0. Between 2.15 and 2.45, Record therefore takes three times as many: 600 to settle and 1200 to measure.
  • The scatter between runs is large here. Repeated 64 × 64 records at T = 2.30, simulated with the sim's own rule, landed anywhere from about 0.1 to 0.6, while at T = 1.6 or 3.0 they repeat to within a few hundredths.
  • That scatter is physics, not noise to be averaged away. The ± in the Record message is the sweep-to-sweep spread, not an error bar.
See itPark a 64 × 64 grid at T = 2.30. Watch for: the M trace drifting slowly and far from zero. At T = 3.0 it stays within about ±0.2.
07

A finite grid blurs the transition

Onsager's curve is for an infinite lattice. An L × L grid cannot show a sharp drop, so its rise is rounded and sits slightly warm of Tc, and some ⟨|M|⟩ remains above it.

The finite-size shift the sim quotes. The amplitude 0.8 is an empirical estimate.
gridapparent Tc⟨|M|⟩ at T = 3.0
32 × 322.326≈ 0.086
64 × 642.298≈ 0.042
96 × 962.288≈ 0.028

Exact Tc = 2.269. The last column is an average of repeated records; a single record scatters by about a third.

  • The tail above Tc falls roughly as 1/L. It is shown, never subtracted.
  • A larger grid gets closer to the exact curve, but near Tc it also needs longer runs.
See itRecord at T = 3.0 on 32, 64, then 96. Watch for: three dots at T = 3.0 that sit lower on the plot as the grid grows.
08

Where it matters

  • One idea, many materials. The order parameter changes name, not role: magnetisation in a magnet, the liquid–vapour density difference in a fluid. Each vanishes at its critical point, and systems that share a dimension and a symmetry share exponents. This is called universality.
  • Real fluids and layered magnets. CO₂ has its liquid–vapour critical point at 304 K and 73.8 bar, in the three-dimensional Ising class (β ≈ 0.326, not this grid's 1/8). Layered magnets such as Rb₂CoF₄ behave as two-dimensional Ising systems, with a measured β close to 1/8.
  • Simulation practice. Metropolis sampling is a standard tool in statistical physics. The slow decisions and finite-size shifts you measured here are the everyday obstacles near any critical point.
Go deeper: how the exponent sets the shape
The leading power law (1 − T/Tc)β, amplitude set to 1, over the last 10% below Tc. Far below Tc neither law holds.
  • Mean-field theory puts the transition at T = 4J/kB (four neighbours), far above the exact 2.269, and gives β = 1/2.
  • Onsager solved the 2D model in 1944. Above two dimensions the exponents come from the renormalisation group and numerics.
09

Summary

In one line. A rule with no preferred direction orders the whole grid below Tc = 2.269 J/kB, which direction wins is chance, and a finite grid blurs the transition.

Key points

  • A flip costs ΔE = 2J si Σ sj. Downhill is always taken, uphill with probability e−ΔE/kBT.
  • Below Tc, ⟨|M|⟩ rises steeply as (1 − T/Tc)1/8.
  • Near Tc the grid decides slowly, so records scatter.
  • A finite L rounds the transition, shifts it warm by about Tc·0.8/L, and leaves a tail that falls as 1/L.

Common mix-ups

  • "Order needs something that favours up." The field is zero and the rule is symmetric. Below Tc, agreeing wins in either direction.
  • "It should settle half up, half down." A wall of mismatched neighbours costs energy. A hasty quench can still freeze into stripes.
  • "The transition on screen is sharp, and ⟨|M|⟩ is zero above it." On a finite grid the rise is rounded, and a tail remains above Tc, about 0.04 on 64 × 64 at T = 3.0.

Things to try on your own

  • Cool slowly from 3.0 and Record at six or more temperatures, then compare your dots with the exact curve.
  • Record three times at T = 2.30, then three times at T = 1.6, and compare the spreads.
  • Record at T = 2.5 on L = 32, 64 and 96 and compare how large the tail above Tc is on each.
